did_you_know.text: Did you know? Chapter 42 opens with Job’s response to the Lord after the Lord’s speeches from the whirlwind. Job no longer argues but acknowledges the Lord’s supremacy and absolute power.
Did you know? Job admits that he spoke about things beyond his understanding: “Things too wonderful for me, which I did not know.” In this way, he recognizes the limits of human knowledge.

Did you know? Job distinguishes between knowing about God through hearing and having a deeper, more direct experience, expressed in the words: “I had heard of you by the hearing of the ear, but now my eye sees you.”

Did you know? At the end of his response, Job expresses repentance and humility in the words, “Therefore I despise myself and repent,” referring to dust and ashes as symbols of his lowly and repentant state.

Did you know? The Lord declares that Job spoke rightly about him—more rightly than his three friends. In this way, the chapter criticizes the friends’ attempt to explain Job’s suffering in simplistic terms.
Did you know? The Lord commands Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar to offer seven bulls and seven rams, and tells them to go to Job so that he can pray for them.
Did you know? Job’s restoration is described as taking place after he prayed for his friends. His family members and acquaintances return to him, eat with him, and comfort him.
Did you know? Those who visit Job give him gifts: each person gives him one kesitah and one gold earring. The verse also describes the renewal of the social ties around him.

Did you know? Job’s daughters—Jemimah, Keziah, and Keren-happuch—are described as the most beautiful women in the land, and the text emphasizes that their father gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers.
Did you know? After the events described in the chapter, Job lived another 140 years and saw his children and grandchildren to the fourth generation.
